ABSTRACT  
Background: Ictal piloerection (IP) is a rare manifestation of focal epilepsy. Autoimmune limbic encephalitis (LE) 
and malignant brain tumours are the most frequent recognized aetiologies. 
Methods: We selected all patients diagnosed with LE in our Institute from 2004 to 2020 and manifesting with IP. 
We performed a literature review on LE patients presenting IP. 
Results: Of 15 patients diagnosed with LE (13.3%), two manifested IP as prominent ictal feature. One of them also 
had stiff-limb syndrome. Video-EEG documented ictal discharges from the right temporal regions with 
concomitant sympathetic skin response (SSR) recording. Antibody testing showed elevated serum and CSF titres 
of GAD65 antibodies (Ab), in both cases. Despite a combination of several anti-seizure medications and first- and 
second-line immunotherapy, they showed a poor clinical outcome after 2 and 9 years of follow-up, respectively. 
The literature review yielded 13 papers reporting 26 LE cases with IP. LGI1 Ab were the most frequently 
associated (73.1%) followed by VGKC-complex (7.7%), GAD65 (7.7%), NMDAr (3.8%), Ma2 (3.8%) and Hu 
(3.8%) Ab. Cases with LGI1 Ab showed a good response to immunotherapy. 
Discussion and conclusion: The prevalence of IP in our LE cohort was of 13.3%, higher than expected. According to 
the literature review, most cases were associated with LGI1 Ab and showed a good response to immunotherapy. 
With the contribution of our cases, GAD65 emerged as the second most frequently detected Ab, showing a poor 
outcome. Our findings widen the spectrum of IP-associated Ab, with the respective prognostic implications.   
1. Introduction 
Ictal piloerection (IP) is a rare manifestation of focal seizures sub -
jectively associated with the sensation of goosebumps or shivers, and it 
may be distributed on one or both sides of the body. Pilomotor seizures 
mainly originate from the mesial temporal lobe. Although the precise 
neural network of IP has not yet been determined, the generator is 
suspected to lie in the insula or amygdala [1] . Previous analysis of the 
“ localising value ” of IP has not given conclusive results. Clearly unilat -
eral IP has been shown to be ipsilateral to the epileptogenic zone [1] , 
whereas a mild prevalence of left temporal lobe seizure onset has been 
reported in bilaterally distributed IP [2] . 
Pilomotor seizures are mostly described in mesial temporal lobe 
epilepsy with underlying structural or autoimmune aetiology. In

particular, malignant brain tumours and limbic encephalitis (LE) are the 
most frequent identifiable causes [ 3 , 4 ]. LE usually manifests as subacute 
onset of cognitive impairment, psychiatric symptoms and seizures. A 
definite diagnosis of autoimmune LE can be achieved only with the 
support of consistent neuroradiological and neurophysiological data, 
including MRI signal abnormalities confined to the medial temporal 
lobes and at least one of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pleocytosis or EEG 
abnormalities in temporal regions [5] . 
The present report provides an in-depth electroclinical characteri -
sation of two cases affected by GAD65 Ab LE with piloerection as a main 
ictal manifestation. Moreover, we performed a literature review focused 
on autoimmune LE manifesting with IP, in order to describe the

2. Methods 
2.1. Case series 
We identified patients referred to our institute from 2004 to 2020 
diagnosed with possible, probable or definite LE and experiencing 
pilomotor seizures. All patients underwent an extensive clinical evalu -
ation, including video-EEG with concomitant sympathetic skin response 
(SSR) recording, brain MRI and CSF analysis. For SSR recording, stan -
dard cup electrodes were applied to the palmar (active) and dorsal 
(reference) surfaces of both hands and, if appropriate, to the soles 
(active) and dorsal surfaces (reference) of the feet. The extremities 
explored (upper/lower) were chosen on the basis of symptom distribu -
tion. The electrodes were connected to a bio-amplifier that recorded 
signals at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz. The band pass filter frequency 
range was 0.3 to 30 Hz, and the sensitivity was set at 0.5 mV/cm. 
Qualitative responses elicited during ictal discharge (stimulus), as 
documented on EEG, were recorded using a standard polygraphic sys -
tem. A response was defined as a change in skin conductance occurring 
during or within 5 s of the end of the stimulus. Antibody testing of both 
serum and CSF was performed. Enzyme linked immunosorbent assay 
(ELISA) was used to test for GAD65 Ab, whereas the presence of onco -
neural Ab was assessed by means of immunofluorescence on brain tissue 
and immunoblot analysis. The presence of LGI1, CASPR2, GABAAR, 
GABABR, NMDAR, AMPAR, DPPX and GlyR Ab, as well as Ab against 
unknown antigens, was assessed by cell-based assay and immunohisto -
chemistry, respectively, as previously described [6] . 
The response to immunomodulatory therapy was evaluated in terms 
of seizure frequency and cognitive outcome after adequate follow up. 
2.2. Literature review 
A PubMed/Medline literature search was conducted using a combi -
nation of the key terms “ encephalitis ” , “ pilomotor ” , “ piloerection ” and 
“ goosebumps ” (Supplemental Material). We applied no restrictions on 
publication date or language, with the exception of the exclusion of 
papers published in Far Eastern languages. The last search was per -
formed in September 2021. The reference lists of the identified articles 
were also reviewed to find additional sources. We excluded reports 
presenting clinical information in the form of aggregate data. Three 
reviewers (FP, MPG, LL) selected the relevant papers through title, ab -
stract and full-text screening. In cases of overlapping data, the most 
recent and comprehensive study was considered. We included cases 
affected by definite, probable or possible autoimmune encephalitis, 
according to the current criteria [5] , and manifesting pilomotor seizures. 
Reports of cases with “ suspected ” LE or IP related to chronic autoim -
mune epilepsies were excluded. 
Data from the identified cases were entered in an ad hoc database 
containing information on clinical history, serological characterisation, 
neuroimaging, CSF analysis, treatment strategies and outcome in terms 
of seizure frequency and psychiatric/cognitive functioning. When 
possible, we contacted the corresponding authors directly to obtain 
relevant missing data. Data on clinical outcome after adequate follow up 
were, when available, carefully reviewed. 
3. Results 
3.1. Case reports 
Among 15 patients from our centre diagnosed with LE, two (13.3%) 
had piloerection as a prominent ictal manifestation.

3.2. Patient 1 
This 24-year-old male patient experienced, at the age of 15 years 
(October 2012), an episode of fever, headache and vomiting, followed 
by subacute onset of episodes characterised by staring and loss of 
awareness, bimanual and oral automatisms, drooling and flushing, 
sometimes preceded by a rising gastric sensation, confusion and lan -
guage difficulties. The episodes occurred multiple times per day. He was 
first admitted to our institute in April 2013. On that occasion, several 
seizures characterised by an initial indefinite sensation, followed by a 
goosebump feeling on the right side of the body, were recorded. During 
the episodes he showed retained awareness, piloerection on the right 
hemisoma, and subsequent bilateral palmar hyperhidrosis, as docu -
mented by SSR recording. Ictal EEG showed right fronto-temporal 
discharge ( Fig. 1 A,B), while interictal EEG showed focal slowing in 
both temporal regions, mainly the left one. Brain MRI showed bilateral 
mesial temporal T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, mainly in the right hippo -
campus, which appeared larger than the contralateral one ( Fig. 1 C,D). 
The results of blood and CSF analyses, which included screening for 
viruses and coeliac disease, and Ab against the neuronal surface antigens 
known at that time (LG1, CASPR2, NMDAR), were unremarkable except 
for the detection of oligoclonal bands. Neuropsychological assessment 
showed a normal total IQ, with a mild discrepancy between verbal and 
performance scores (worse on verbal IQ). He was started on carbamaz -
epine and clobazam and obtained partial seizure control. Over the 
following years seizure frequency remained stable (0 – 2/month) but 
memory and concentration problems progressively emerged. At the age 
of 21 years (February 2018) the patient was again admitted to our 
institute since he had started experiencing brief episodes of stiffness of 
the left arm and leg while walking, or triggered by tapping. At that time, 
GAD65 Ab were detected at high titres in both serum (1,230,275 IU/ml) 
and CSF (171,180 IU/ml). Onconeural and neuronal surface Ab, 
including GlyR and amphiphysin, were negative. EMG showed syn -
chronous contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles of the left upper 
limb, allowing diagnosis of stiff limb syndrome (SLS). Paraneoplastic 
aetiology was ruled out (chest and abdominal CT, testicular ultrasound 
and total body FDG-PET were unremarkable). 
In the same period, seizure frequency had progressively increased up 
to multiple episodes per week. 
The patient underwent first- and second-line immunotherapy (IV 
steroids, IVIg, PLEX, rituximab) without substantial clinical improve -
ment and with persistence of high GAD65 Ab titres. Currently, in spite of 
trying several combinations of antiseizure medications (ASMs), he 
continues to have multiple seizures per month and presents cognitive 
impairment with long-term, verbal and visuospatial memory deficits. 
3.3. Patient 2 
This 32-year-old woman was first admitted to our institute at the age 
of 30 (January 2020) due to the acute onset of episodes characterised by 
d ´ej `a vu, nausea, unpleasant olfactory sensation, supraorbital pain on the 
right side, and a goosebump feeling on the right arm with retained 
awareness. The episodes, lasting a few seconds, occurred multiple times 
per day. Right temporal ictal discharge was observed on EEG, while SSR 
recording documented increased electrodermal activity involving both

hands ( Fig. 2 A,B). Brain MRI showed bilateral mesial temporal T2 
hyperintensity and enlargement of the right hippocampus, with contrast 
enhancement ( Fig. 2 C,D). CSF analysis showed mild pleocytosis (14 
white blood cells/mm
3
). GAD65 Ab were detected in both serum 
(49,700 IU/ml) and CSF (2.3 IU/ml). Otherwise, screening for autoim -
mune Ab was negative. Despite trying several associations of ASMs 
(PHT, LEV, LTG, CLB) and high-dose steroid therapy, the patient ob -
tained an only mild improvement of seizures (reduction in frequency 
from 15 to 10 per day). After discharge, despite IVIg cycles, her condi -
tion remained stable. In May 2020, she reported an increase in seizure 
frequency, with bilaterally distributed IP and mild memory and

Rituximab treatment was attempted and lacosamide was introduced, but 
the patient showed no substantial clinical changes. At age 32 years

persistent feeling of unreality and alienation, suggestive of non -

evident paroxysmal changes during the episode that, however, resolved 
after oral administration of clonazepam. Moreover, interictal EEG 
showed sharp waves over the right temporal region. At this time, the 
right hippocampal alterations, although milder than before, were still 
visible on brain MRI, whereas laboratory tests showed higher GAD65 Ab 
titres in both serum and CSF (increased to 91,550 IU/ml and 412 IU/ml, 
respectively). Neuropsychological testing revealed visuospatial memory 
impairment. Therefore, a combination of oral steroids (50 mg/day fol -
lowed by slow tapering) and mycophenolate mofetil (1500 mg/day) was 
introduced. After a free interval of about five months, her seizures 
reappeared with the same semeiology and with almost daily frequency. 
3.4. Literature review 
Overall, 13 papers [ 3 , 4 , 7 – 17 ], referring to a total of 26 cases, were 
identified ( Fig. 3 ). Further data on some of the included cases, reported 
in a single paper [3] , were collected thanks to the cooperation of the 
corresponding author. Table. 1 summarizes the demographic and 
clinical features of the 26 included patients (10 females, 40%). A list of 
all the papers retrieved is provided in the Supplemental Material. 
The mean age at disease onset was 47.2 years (range: 26 – 71). In 8/26 
(30.8%) patients, piloerection was not the only ictal manifestation, 
being associated with other autonomic, sensory and emotional symp -
toms. IP distribution was unilateral in 7/12 (58.3%) cases. In 4/6 
(66.7%), IP was contralateral to the epileptogenic zone. Pilomotor 
seizure frequency was daily or multiple per day in all cases. In 7/26 
(26.9%) patients, both interictal and ictal EEG recordings were unre -
markable. Brain MRI showed bilateral mesial temporal inflammatory 
alterations in 6/23 (26.1%) patients. In the sample as a whole, the 
following Ab were detected: LGI1 in 19/26 (73.1%) cases, VGKC in 2/26 
(7.7%), GAD65 in 2/26 (7.7%), NMDAr in 1/26 (3.8%), Ma2 in 1/26 
(3.8%) and Hu in 1/26 (3.8%), as shown in Fig. 4 . 
Outcome data were available in 24/26 (92.3%) cases. Twenty of 
them (83.3%) showed symptoms of improvement or complete resolu -
tion: of these, 17/20 (85.0%) had LGI1, 2/20 (10.0%) VGKC-complex, 
and 1/20 (5.0%) NMDAr Ab. In the remaining 4 (16.7%) cases the 
clinical manifestations remained unchanged: of these, 2/4 (50.0%) 
showed GAD65, 1/4 (25.0%) Hu, and 1/4 (25.0%) Ma2 Ab.

comprehensively reviewed all reports of LE with IP present in the 
literature to date. 
Although the exact prevalence of pilomotor seizures in LE is un -
known, piloerection is still considered a rare ictal manifestation of focal 
epilepsy, with an estimated prevalence of 0.65% [3] . However, 
considering that IP is a subtle sign that may go unnoticed and should be 
actively searched by the clinician, its prevalence could be under -
estimated. In fact, in our local cohort of patients diagnosed with LE, we 
found a pilomotor seizure prevalence of 13.3%, in line with the IP 
prevalence we extrapolated from the LE cohorts described by Finke et al. 
[16] and McGinty et al. [8] (13.3% and 14%, respectively). 
Both of our patients were affected by LE associated with GAD65 Ab. 
Among cases with LE and IP described in the literature, LGI1 and VGKC- 
complex Ab were the types most frequently reported (80.8%). Although 
the specific target was not investigated, also in the VGKC-complex 
seropositive cases the Ab were likely directed against LGI1 or CASPR2 
[ 18 , 19 ]. By contrast, GAD65 Ab were found in less than 10%. An 
additional report in which IP was associated with GAD65 Ab was 
excluded from our analysis as the patient in question had chronic re -
fractory epilepsy of suspected autoimmune aetiology not fulfilling the 
criteria for LE [20] . 
The two LE cases with GAD65 Ab identified through the literature 
review showed a poor outcome, displaying pharmacoresistant epilepsy 
and progressive cognitive impairment [4] . Although it should be noted 
that both were likely undertreated, these observations are in line with 
current knowledge on the prognosis of GAD65 Ab-related LE [21] . Our 
patient 1 showed a similar unfavourable disease course, even though we 
cannot exclude that this was related to the delayed diagnosis and initi -
ation of immune treatment. In fact, he did not receive a definite diag -
nosis until six years after disease onset, when the emergence of SLS 
raised the suspicion of a GAD65 Ab-related pathogenesis. That said, 
patient 2, despite receiving prompt first- and second-line immunother -
apies and multiple ASMs, still experiences memory impairment and 
daily seizures. 
In our two patients IP was unilaterally distributed on the right side of 
the body, ipsilateral to the epileptic discharge on EEG and to the pre -
dominantly affected mesial temporal lobe, in accordance with the 
findings of Loddenkemper et al. [1] . Instead, among the cases from our 
literature review in which IP localisation was reported, most showed 
(66.7%) a contralateral distribution. 
To our knowledge, our two case reports are the first to include 
investigation of SSR during IP. SSR is defined as a temporary change in 
the electrical skin potential (or electrodermal activity, EDA), reflecting 
the activation of sympathetic cholinergic sudomotor function [22] . 
Our patients showed a brief, transient change in EDA which, of note, 
occurred at the end of the ictal discharge and bilaterally. In previous 
reports, EDA increase during seizures was most evident in the postictal 
phase of generalized tonic-clonic seizures, due to sympathetic hyper -
arousal [23] . Data on focal seizures are scant, but we might speculate 
that changes in EDA are greater in seizures with prominent autonomic

sympathetic features such as piloerection and, therefore that EDA 
recording might be useful to detect this subtle ictal manifestation. The 
detection of IP could be relevant since it could guide, after the exclusion 
of structural lesions (i.e., tumours), the search for an autoimmune 
aetiology also in cases without all the clinical features typically associ -
ated with LE. In fact, a recent study showed an association between IP 
and Ab against neuronal surface antigens in patients with new-onset 
focal epilepsy [8] . This observation is in line with our cases, who pre -
sented seizures but no cognitive impairment, movement disorders or 
focal neurological deficits. Our data suggest that the spectrum of Ab to 
test in these cases should include GAD65-Ab. 
The search for VGKC-complex Ab is no longer advised and patients 
should be tested for Ab against specific targets (CASPR2 and LGI1) 
instead [ 18 , 19 ]. 
5. Conclusions 
The prevalence of IP in autoimmune LE could be higher than pre -
viously thought. To facilitate its detection, SSR recording could be 
included in the electrophysiological study of patients with suspected LE. 
Considering our cases together with the literature data, GAD65 
emerged as the second most frequently detected Ab in patients affected 
by LE and pilomotor seizures. This finding widens the spectrum of Ab 
associated with this ictal phenomenon, and the respective prognostic 
implications.

This 24-year-old male patient experienced, at the age of 15 years 
(October 2012), an episode of fever, headache and vomiting, followed 
by subacute onset of episodes characterised by staring and loss of 
awareness, bimanual and oral automatisms, drooling and flushing, 
sometimes preceded by a rising gastric sensation, confusion and lan -
guage difficulties. The episodes occurred multiple times per day. He was 
first admitted to our institute in April 2013. On that occasion, several 
seizures characterised by an initial indefinite sensation, followed by a 
goosebump feeling on the right side of the body, were recorded. During 
the episodes he showed retained awareness, piloerection on the right 
hemisoma, and subsequent bilateral palmar hyperhidrosis, as docu -
mented by SSR recording. Ictal EEG showed right fronto-temporal 
discharge ( Fig. 1 A,B), while interictal EEG showed focal slowing in 
both temporal regions, mainly the left one. Brain MRI showed bilateral 
mesial temporal T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, mainly in the right hippo -
campus, which appeared larger than the contralateral one ( Fig. 1 C,D). 
The results of blood and CSF analyses, which included screening for 
viruses and coeliac disease, and Ab against the neuronal surface antigens 
known at that time (LG1, CASPR2, NMDAR), were unremarkable except 
for the detection of oligoclonal bands. Neuropsychological assessment 
showed a normal total IQ, with a mild discrepancy between verbal and 
performance scores (worse on verbal IQ). He was started on carbamaz -
epine and clobazam and obtained partial seizure control. Over the 
following years seizure frequency remained stable (0 – 2/month) but 
memory and concentration problems progressively emerged. At the age 
of 21 years (February 2018) the patient was again admitted to our 
institute since he had started experiencing brief episodes of stiffness of 
the left arm and leg while walking, or triggered by tapping. At that time, 
GAD65 Ab were detected at high titres in both serum (1,230,275 IU/ml) 
and CSF (171,180 IU/ml). Onconeural and neuronal surface Ab, 
including GlyR and amphiphysin, were negative. EMG showed syn -
chronous contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles of the left upper 
limb, allowing diagnosis of stiff limb syndrome (SLS). Paraneoplastic 
aetiology was ruled out (chest and abdominal CT, testicular ultrasound 
and total body FDG-PET were unremarkable). 
In the same period, seizure frequency had progressively increased up 
to multiple episodes per week. 
The patient underwent first- and second-line immunotherapy (IV 
steroids, IVIg, PLEX, rituximab) without substantial clinical improve -
ment and with persistence of high GAD65 Ab titres. Currently, in spite of 
trying several combinations of antiseizure medications (ASMs), he 
continues to have multiple seizures per month and presents cognitive 
impairment with long-term, verbal and visuospatial memory deficits. 
3.3. Patient 2 
This 32-year-old woman was first admitted to our institute at the age 
of 30 (January 2020) due to the acute onset of episodes characterised by 
d ´ej `a vu, nausea, unpleasant olfactory sensation, supraorbital pain on the 
right side, and a goosebump feeling on the right arm with retained 
awareness. The episodes, lasting a few seconds, occurred multiple times 
per day. Right temporal ictal discharge was observed on EEG, while SSR 
recording documented increased electrodermal activity involving both

hands ( Fig. 2 A,B). Brain MRI showed bilateral mesial temporal T2 
hyperintensity and enlargement of the right hippocampus, with contrast 
enhancement ( Fig. 2 C,D). CSF analysis showed mild pleocytosis (14 
white blood cells/mm
3
). GAD65 Ab were detected in both serum 
(49,700 IU/ml) and CSF (2.3 IU/ml). Otherwise, screening for autoim -
mune Ab was negative. Despite trying several associations of ASMs 
(PHT, LEV, LTG, CLB) and high-dose steroid therapy, the patient ob -
tained an only mild improvement of seizures (reduction in frequency 
from 15 to 10 per day). After discharge, despite IVIg cycles, her condi -
tion remained stable. In May 2020, she reported an increase in seizure 
frequency, with bilaterally distributed IP and mild memory and

language impairment. A new brain MRI showed persistence of the pre -
viously observed T2 hyperintensity and right hippocampal enlargement. 
Rituximab treatment was attempted and lacosamide was introduced, but 
the patient showed no substantial clinical changes. At age 32 years 
(March 2021), she was urgently readmitted to our institute with a 
persistent feeling of unreality and alienation, suggestive of non -
convulsive status epilepticus. Prolonged EEG monitoring did not show 
evident paroxysmal changes during the episode that, however, resolved 
after oral administration of clonazepam. Moreover, interictal EEG 
showed sharp waves over the right temporal region. At this time, the 
right hippocampal alterations, although milder than before, were still 
visible on brain MRI, whereas laboratory tests showed higher GAD65 Ab 
titres in both serum and CSF (increased to 91,550 IU/ml and 412 IU/ml, 
respectively). Neuropsychological testing revealed visuospatial memory 
impairment. Therefore, a combination of oral steroids (50 mg/day fol -
lowed by slow tapering) and mycophenolate mofetil (1500 mg/day) was 
introduced. After a free interval of about five months, her seizures 
reappeared with the same semeiology and with almost daily frequency. 
3.4. Literature review 
Overall, 13 papers [ 3 , 4 , 7 – 17 ], referring to a total of 26 cases, were 
identified ( Fig. 3 ). Further data on some of the included cases, reported 
in a single paper [3] , were collected thanks to the cooperation of the 
corresponding author. Table. 1 summarizes the demographic and 
clinical features of the 26 included patients (10 females, 40%). A list of 
all the papers retrieved is provided in the Supplemental Material. 
The mean age at disease onset was 47.2 years (range: 26 – 71). In 8/26 
(30.8%) patients, piloerection was not the only ictal manifestation, 
being associated with other autonomic, sensory and emotional symp -
toms. IP distribution was unilateral in 7/12 (58.3%) cases. In 4/6 
(66.7%), IP was contralateral to the epileptogenic zone. Pilomotor 
seizure frequency was daily or multiple per day in all cases. In 7/26 
(26.9%) patients, both interictal and ictal EEG recordings were unre -
markable. Brain MRI showed bilateral mesial temporal inflammatory 
alterations in 6/23 (26.1%) patients. In the sample as a whole, the 
following Ab were detected: LGI1 in 19/26 (73.1%) cases, VGKC in 2/26 
(7.7%), GAD65 in 2/26 (7.7%), NMDAr in 1/26 (3.8%), Ma2 in 1/26 
(3.8%) and Hu in 1/26 (3.8%), as shown in Fig. 4 . 
Outcome data were available in 24/26 (92.3%) cases. Twenty of 
them (83.3%) showed symptoms of improvement or complete resolu -
tion: of these, 17/20 (85.0%) had LGI1, 2/20 (10.0%) VGKC-complex, 
and 1/20 (5.0%) NMDAr Ab. In the remaining 4 (16.7%) cases the 
clinical manifestations remained unchanged: of these, 2/4 (50.0%) 
showed GAD65, 1/4 (25.0%) Hu, and 1/4 (25.0%) Ma2 Ab.

segments.text:
Seizure: European Journal of Epilepsy 98 (2022) 71–78
77
pilomotor seizures; as well as describing these novel cases, we 
comprehensively reviewed all reports of LE with IP present in the 
literature to date. 
Although the exact prevalence of pilomotor seizures in LE is un -
known, piloerection is still considered a rare ictal manifestation of focal 
epilepsy, with an estimated prevalence of 0.65% [3] . However, 
considering that IP is a subtle sign that may go unnoticed and should be 
actively searched by the clinician, its prevalence could be under -
estimated. In fact, in our local cohort of patients diagnosed with LE, we 
found a pilomotor seizure prevalence of 13.3%, in line with the IP 
prevalence we extrapolated from the LE cohorts described by Finke et al. 
[16] and McGinty et al. [8] (13.3% and 14%, respectively). 
Both of our patients were affected by LE associated with GAD65 Ab. 
Among cases with LE and IP described in the literature, LGI1 and VGKC- 
complex Ab were the types most frequently reported (80.8%). Although 
the specific target was not investigated, also in the VGKC-complex 
seropositive cases the Ab were likely directed against LGI1 or CASPR2 
[ 18 , 19 ]. By contrast, GAD65 Ab were found in less than 10%. An 
additional report in which IP was associated with GAD65 Ab was 
excluded from our analysis as the patient in question had chronic re -
fractory epilepsy of suspected autoimmune aetiology not fulfilling the 
criteria for LE [20] . 
The two LE cases with GAD65 Ab identified through the literature 
review showed a poor outcome, displaying pharmacoresistant epilepsy 
and progressive cognitive impairment [4] . Although it should be noted 
that both were likely undertreated, these observations are in line with 
current knowledge on the prognosis of GAD65 Ab-related LE [21] . Our 
patient 1 showed a similar unfavourable disease course, even though we 
cannot exclude that this was related to the delayed diagnosis and initi -
ation of immune treatment. In fact, he did not receive a definite diag -
nosis until six years after disease onset, when the emergence of SLS 
raised the suspicion of a GAD65 Ab-related pathogenesis. That said, 
patient 2, despite receiving prompt first- and second-line immunother -
apies and multiple ASMs, still experiences memory impairment and 
daily seizures. 
In our two patients IP was unilaterally distributed on the right side of 
the body, ipsilateral to the epileptic discharge on EEG and to the pre -
dominantly affected mesial temporal lobe, in accordance with the 
findings of Loddenkemper et al. [1] . Instead, among the cases from our 
literature review in which IP localisation was reported, most showed 
(66.7%) a contralateral distribution. 
To our knowledge, our two case reports are the first to include 
investigation of SSR during IP. SSR is defined as a temporary change in 
the electrical skin potential (or electrodermal activity, EDA), reflecting 
the activation of sympathetic cholinergic sudomotor function [22] . 
Our patients showed a brief, transient change in EDA which, of note, 
occurred at the end of the ictal discharge and bilaterally. In previous 
reports, EDA increase during seizures was most evident in the postictal 
phase of generalized tonic-clonic seizures, due to sympathetic hyper -
arousal [23] . Data on focal seizures are scant, but we might speculate 
that changes in EDA are greater in seizures with prominent autonomic
segments.evidence: Deterministic clinical-window selection for Stage 07 single-case v1.

segments.text:
sympathetic features such as piloerection and, therefore that EDA 
recording might be useful to detect this subtle ictal manifestation. The 
detection of IP could be relevant since it could guide, after the exclusion 
of structural lesions (i.e., tumours), the search for an autoimmune 
aetiology also in cases without all the clinical features typically associ -
ated with LE. In fact, a recent study showed an association between IP 
and Ab against neuronal surface antigens in patients with new-onset 
focal epilepsy [8] . This observation is in line with our cases, who pre -
sented seizures but no cognitive impairment, movement disorders or 
focal neurological deficits. Our data suggest that the spectrum of Ab to 
test in these cases should include GAD65-Ab. 
The search for VGKC-complex Ab is no longer advised and patients 
should be tested for Ab against specific targets (CASPR2 and LGI1) 
instead [ 18 , 19 ]. 
5. Conclusions 
The prevalence of IP in autoimmune LE could be higher than pre -
viously thought. To facilitate its detection, SSR recording could be 
included in the electrophysiological study of patients with suspected LE. 
Considering our cases together with the literature data, GAD65 
emerged as the second most frequently detected Ab in patients affected 
by LE and pilomotor seizures. This finding widens the spectrum of Ab 
associated with this ictal phenomenon, and the respective prognostic 
implications.
